item.content:encoded:
This is something that ticks all of my boxes. Historical, the Factory, political, rooted in a place and time, fools being overtaken by forces beyond their control, plenty of esoteric window dressing, eldritch abominations that only consume, body horror, etc.

At absolutely no point, however, was I excited. Probably it was at the listing of products that I started to lose interest, as it struck me as overly similar to 186 (not a fair comparison, I know, but "early 20th century thing that does another, horrible thing, with aid from mysterious spooky dood, also lots of telegrams and diary entries" was covered pretty definitively by that article, imo).

As soon as I realized that it was the Factory, the rest of the article fell into place. Of course there would be some entity dude with a vague and/or capitalized name. Of course the workers would be ground up into garmonbozia. Of course Metzger would get fucked over by his partner. And so on. It's not a bad model, but it's a story that I feel like I've read before (see: Bright's proposal, 186, some of the more esoteric interpretations of Dark).

While I don't mind the idea of The Factory as a SCP, I wonder about the narrative limitations of the Factory as a GoI, as they are, almost by definition, going to be rapacious, evil, uncaring, inhuman simulacrum/perfect realization of capitalism. Which is good as far as it goes, but there's a limited amount that you can do with just "disembodied, impersonal thing that doesn't understand how people function." I feel like this article has hit that limit pretty hard.

While I salute the monumental amounts of effort and moxie that it took to make this, I don't actually enjoy it as an article. -1

item.title: Re: Capitalism? Communism? ISMism?
item.content:encoded:
From my end it looks like a straightforward critique of capitalism. I don't know what a "uni force" is, but communism as a 'social ideal' doesn't desire or require bosses, slave labor, sale of goods on the market…

As for fascism, The Factory seems completely disinterested in war or nationalism, and we see nothing of how it deals with a hypothetical working population (for all we know, its harvesters are automatons), so fascism is out of the picture.

"Comitascism" is literally just a nasty form of capitalism, with regards to how people relate to each other and how production is organized. The employer being the same as the people who sell you food is just a company town.

"Capital is dead labor which, vampire-like, lives only by sucking living labor, and lives the more, the more labor it sucks. —Karl Marx, Capital."

If I had to describe The Factory in social terms, it would be as fully undead labor: rather than being animated by the labor of living workers, this apparatus of production and resource collection has animated itself; free from the restraints imposed by the employment of humans (any capitalist's wet dream), it can do strange and terrifying things.

item.title: Capitalism? Communism? ISMism?
item.content:encoded:
The SCP itself is truly interesting, well written and kind of believable. Though I do notice the social commentary and find that it does not fit any social ideal I know of.

It takes consumer and producer from capitalism, the uni force from communism, and the join or die from fascism (at least that is what I observe). So what is it? Well, as I do not think there exist an as yet classified system in this manner, I have taken the liberty of making my own classification:

I declare it Fapunism….a few seconds after I wrote that I started thinking "why does that seem weird?" Thus, I have changed it to Comitascism.

Comitascism is a government that basically taxes by product. They sell you food, but they also pay you. Not only that, but those who fall bellow the productivity marker, or are deemed unfit, are turned into products themselves. It is all of the worst from two of the worst (commies and fascies) and the best (capitalism), but so much worse. Just goes to show: with the right mixture, you can kill a man with water and lime juice. (that was a metaphor)

item.title: Provenance
item.content:encoded:
The photo of the bearded man is from https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Christian_Michelsen_OB.F04667.jpg ; Christian Michelsen was the first Prime Minister of Norway and the photo is from 1908 (and thus is public domain).

The smokestack is from https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Abandoned_textile_industry_factory_in_Porto.jpg , taken in 2009 by Francisco Restivo and released as Creative Commons on Flickr; edited into b/w by Metaphysician.

The brain is from https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Human_brain_in_a_vat.jpg , taken 2007 by Gaetan Lee. He originally made it available under Creative Commons on Flickr, but subsequently changed that to "All Rights Reserved"; however, Creative Commons cannot be revoked.

The sparkly golden machine thingy is a chopped-and-mashed version of a photo of Babbage's difference engine.

item.content:encoded:
While I understand where you are coming from, I'm going to keep it as is. I didn't want to imply that The Factory, when fully active, was something the Foundation (at the time) could really contain. Thus, containment is focused on containing or neutralizing products until the Foundation is able to figure out a way of containing the full anomaly.

At the time of the Keter iteration, the Foundation is still scrambling to deal with the problem - so was writing from the point of view of that time.

Edit: Probably didn't explain this well at all but tired;/

Edit 2: Or it other words, I didn't want to be the one to cage the Factory;p Once the other "748" connect, it more or less functions as a pocket plane. SCP-748 is now more or less one entrance to something vast and constantly changing.

I did struggle with this actually and was originally going to have the Foundation recapture 748 but now be aware of the greater whole but I felt it would go against my idea of them coming together again as a single entity. In my head, Factory products were primarily encountered in the early 1900s but slowly stopped appearing in shops as it was dismantled by the Investor. The few encountered after this time were from remnant shops similar to 748 but still able to function to a degree (so, the products likely popping up close to that "748", which itself is probably hidden underground) or items that were created in the early 1900s-1940s that were simply rediscovered (the item likely purchased and then abandoned, or causing the death of its owner and never recognized as anomalous by others).

Once the Factory reestablishes connection, entities like SCP-748-4 ("managers") become more or less part of a swarm intelligence. Stopping it now would have required something akin to reality anchors and didn't want to go in that direction. Too easy.

In my mind, I also suspect that they will now become a bit more adaptive. Expect to see some pop-ups and spam emails about Factory products ;p Didn't want to touch that, clashed with the *feel* but, I imagine them altering themselves to gain more consumers. "Everything is on internetwebs these days!" shouts a brain in a jar;p

item.title: Word change
item.content:encoded:
Hopefully this isn't seen as me overstepping in terms of edits, but I changed "energy" to "power" when describing what the machines needed to operate. Yes, machinery do need energy, but they also need so much energy getting at them in so much time in order to operate. This is why motors are rated in horsepowers and electrodomestics are rated in watts: they'll deliver/use a certain amount of energy in a given amount of time.

Power is simply energy/time, and that's why fusion reactors excel: it's not just that they produce a lot of energy, it's that they produce a lot of eneryg in relatively short amounts of time.

Anyways, I really enjoyed this. It's not as esoteric as I have The Factory in my headcanon, but it's still a great description.

item.content:encoded:
A couple of small things first: the section with the greek names starts by referring to four machines, although only three are named and the the last is noted as missing (as an aside, I think those first three footnotes could be combined into one). Later there is a "causalities" which I think should be "casualties".

This has a lot of very good writing, but for me the overall effect is slightly underwhelming. Perhaps it is that it reads like an SCP greatest hits: mysterious location, complex machinery, changing structural layout / spatial anomalies, ominous backstory / puppetmaster, revelatory notes, brains in jars, humanoid monstrosities with no/changed faces, human/mechanical body horror, "oh no it's Keter", more revelatory notes, GoI. Perhaps it's the fact that the diary scraps in particular are so flatly expositional - the characters were so directly exposing their feelings that they didn't feel real or become immersive.

Or perhaps I'm just jealous of a new Series I article that explains a piece of site canon using brains in jars, and is successful. I'm upvoting, because this is well written and is mostly solid worldbuilding. But I think it would be improved by deleting the very final Addendum (or even the whole collapsible in which it's contained), and by revisiting the diary scraps with a view to humanising them (or even deleting them - I'm not sure what the SCP loses by doing that).
